captions: Hello, and welcome to Camday English, Stage 9. In this lesson: The vanishing bees.
Read an investigative report and distinguish fact, opinion and speculation.
Here are some new words. Investigate. Examine something carefully to discover the truth. Decline.
A fall in amount or quality. Pesticide. A chemical used to kill insects that damage crops.
And some more words. Pollinate. Carry pollen from one flower to another. Speculation.
Guesses about something without full evidence. Source. A person or document that gives information.
Time for a question. The video will stop.
Which word means: examine something carefully to discover the truth?
Now some grammar: Fact, opinion and speculation. A fact can be checked. An opinion is a belief or feeling.
Speculation is a guess about what may be true, often with may, might, could or possibly.
For example: Fact: Bee numbers fell by 30 phần trăm last year.
For example: Opinion: This is the most worrying problem we face.
For example: Speculation: Pesticides may be partly to blame.
Now listen, and read along. Where have all the bees gone?
In the hills outside Valmont, beekeeper Rosa Delgado opens a hive and shakes her head.
‘Last spring, this box was full,’ she says. ‘Now look – maybe a few hundred bees.’ Rosa is not alone.
Our investigation,
which included interviews with twenty-three beekeepers and data from the regional farming office,
found that bee colonies in the area fell by around 30 phần trăm in two years.
The cause is not fully understood.
Several scientists we spoke to believe a group of pesticides may be partly responsible.
Others point to disease, habitat loss and unusually hot summers.
It is likely that more than one factor is involved.
The stakes are high.
Bees pollinate around a third of the food we eat, including apples, almonds and tomatoes.
A spokesperson for the largest pesticide manufacturer said its products were ‘safe when used correctly’,
and added that there was ‘no clear evidence’ linking them to the decline. Rosa is not convinced.
‘Something has changed,’ she says. ‘And the bees are paying the price.’
Another question. The video will stop. How many beekeepers were interviewed?
Well done! Today you learned new words, like investigate, decline, pesticide.
You practised fact, opinion and speculation. And you read Where have all the bees gone?
Now try the practice questions. See you next time!

captions: Hello, and welcome to Camday English, Stage 9. In this lesson: Spotting bias.
Identify bias in reporting and use passive forms with modal verbs.
Here are some new words. Bias. Unfairly supporting one side. Objective. Based on facts, not feelings.
Subjective. Based on personal feelings and opinions.
And some more words. Loaded language. Words chosen to create a strong positive or negative feeling.
Balanced. Giving fair attention to all sides. Omit. Leave something out.
Time for a question. The video will stop. Which word means: unfairly supporting one side?
Now some grammar: Passive with modal verbs.
Use modal plus be plus past participle: must be done, should be checked, can be seen, could be improved.
Reports use it to sound objective. For example: All facts should be checked.
For example: The decision can't be changed. For example: More research must be carried out.
Now listen, and read along. Two reports, one event.
Report A: Hundreds of angry protesters stormed the city centre yesterday, causing chaos for shoppers.
The selfish demonstrators blocked roads for hours,
demanding the council scrap its plans for a new car park on Green Lane Park.
Report B: Around 400 residents marched peacefully through the city centre
yesterday to protest against plans to build a car park on Green Lane Park.
Some roads were closed for two hours. A council spokesperson said the plans would be reviewed,
while a local shop owner said the closures had been ‘frustrating’ for business.
Another question. The video will stop. How does Report A describe the protesters?
Well done! Today you learned new words, like bias, objective, subjective.
You practised passive with modal verbs. And you read Two reports, one event. Now try the practice questions.
See you next time!
